subject: Cognitive Science
title: ADHD: When Attention Breaks
description: A fast breakdown of ADHD: When Attention Breaks for builders.

hook.text: A child who can hyperfocus on video games for hours but can't sit through five minutes of homework. That's ADHD.

buildup.text: ADHD isn't a lack of attention—it's a problem with regulating attention. The steering is broken, not the engine.

discovery.text: Brain scans show reduced dopamine signaling in the prefrontal cortex, weakening executive control.

twist.text: Stimulant medications seem paradoxical—they speed up the brain to calm it down. But they boost the weak dopamine signal.

climax.text: ADHD affects 5–7% of children worldwide and often persists into adulthood, reshaping careers and relationships.

punchline.text: ADHD isn't too little attention—it's attention without a rudder.

quiz.question: What is the core problem in ADHD?

details.summary: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition involving persistent difficulty with sustained attention, impulse control, and executive function. It affects roughly 5 to 7 percent of children and often persists into adulthood.
details.whyItMatters: ADHD shows what happens when the attention system's biological infrastructure is disrupted. Understanding it reduces stigma and improves treatment, affecting millions worldwide.
takeaways: ADHD involves deficits in attention, impulse control, and executive function
It affects 5 to 7 percent of children and often persists into adulthood
Dopamine and norepinephrine systems are centrally involved

faq.question: Is ADHD a real neurological condition or just laziness?
faq.answer: ADHD is a well-established neurological condition with measurable brain differences. Neuroimaging shows reduced prefrontal cortex activity and altered dopamine systems. It is recognized by every major medical organization worldwide. Framing it as laziness is both inaccurate and harmful.

faq.question: Can adults develop ADHD or is it only a childhood condition?
faq.answer: ADHD begins in childhood but persists into adulthood in about 60 percent of cases. Many adults are diagnosed late because childhood symptoms were misattributed to personality traits. Adult ADHD presents as disorganization, restlessness, and difficulty with sustained attention.
